nameStory: Bluemink gets its name from the soft, fluffy texture of its tiny flowers, which cluster together like the plush fur of a blue mink coat. The individual flowers are so small and densely packed that they create a velvety appearance that's irresistible to touch. It's also called flossflower because the blooms look like tufts of colored dental floss bundled together.
description: Bluemink is a low-growing annual flower that forms neat, rounded mounds about 6-12 inches tall and wide. It produces clusters of tiny, fluffy flowers that are typically blue, purple, pink, or white, creating a soft, cushion-like appearance. The small, heart-shaped leaves are slightly fuzzy and have a pleasant, mild scent when brushed. This popular garden plant blooms continuously from spring until the first frost, making it a favorite for flower beds and containers.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny tubular flowers packed into dense, fluffy clusters that feel soft and spongy to the touch, lacking the typical petals you'd expect from the daisy family

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, heart-shaped leaves with slightly fuzzy surfaces arranged in opposite pairs along the stem, releasing a mild, sweet scent when crushed

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms compact, mounded clumps that stay neat and tidy without spreading aggressively, typically 6-12 inches tall and wide

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Flower clusters are about 1-2 inches across and feel remarkably soft, like tiny pompoms, with colors ranging from blue to purple, pink, or white

habitat: In New England, bluemink is found almost exclusively in cultivated settings like flower gardens, container plantings, and park landscapes. It prefers well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade and thrives in the cool, moist conditions of New England summers. You won't typically find it naturalized in wild areas, as it's primarily grown as an ornamental bedding plant.

seasonality.spring: Young plants appear in gardens after the last frost, with small heart-shaped leaves and compact growth habit. Early flower buds begin forming as weather warms.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with abundant fluffy flower clusters in full display. Plants maintain their neat, mounded shape and continue producing new flowers throughout the season.
seasonality.fall: Continues blooming vigorously until the first hard frost, often outlasting many other annual flowers. Seeds may begin forming in older flower clusters.
seasonality.winter: Plants are killed by frost and disappear completely, leaving no winter presence since this is a non-hardy annual.

funFact: Despite being in the daisy family, bluemink flowers have no petals at all – what looks like a fluffy flower cluster is actually made up of dozens of tiny tubes, each one a complete flower that's perfectly designed to attract butterflies with its landing-pad shape and continuous nectar supply.
confusionNotes: Bluemink might be confused with other small, clustered flowers like sweet alyssum, but bluemink's flowers are distinctly fluffy and tube-shaped rather than having four flat petals. Remember: if it feels like a tiny pompom, it's likely bluemink; if it has obvious individual petals, look elsewhere.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'flossflower' can be confusing because it doesn't refer to the actual floss flower (Amsonia), which is a completely different native perennial. Bluemink is also sometimes called 'goatweed,' but this name is shared with several other unrelated plants, so it's best to stick with bluemink or flossflower when discussing this species.
compareHints: Bluemink is the only Ageratum species commonly grown in New England gardens. Within the larger daisy family, it's quite distinctive due to its lack of typical ray petals (the white 'petals' of a daisy). Unlike true daisies or asters, bluemink flowers are all tubes clustered together, giving it that characteristic soft, fluffy appearance that sets it apart from its relatives.
